nameStory: Red campion gets its name from its bright rose-red flowers and its old association with military camps, where soldiers would gather these hardy wildflowers. The word 'campion' likely comes from the Latin 'campus' meaning field, reflecting how these cheerful blooms pop up in open meadows and disturbed ground where people have passed through.
description: Red campion is a charming European wildflower that has made itself at home in New England's countryside. This herbaceous perennial grows 1-3 feet tall with soft, hairy stems and produces clusters of bright pink to rose-red flowers from late spring through summer. The plant forms loose, bushy clumps with oval leaves arranged in pairs along the stems, creating an overall cottage garden appearance that brightens meadows and roadsides.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright pink to rose-red flowers with 5 deeply notched petals that look almost heart-shaped, each about an inch across with a inflated, balloon-like base (calyx) behind the petals

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, covered with fine hairs that give them a velvety texture when you rub them between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose, bushy clumps 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel slightly sticky to the touch

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, oval seed capsules that split open at the top with tiny teeth, releasing dark seeds that rattle inside when mature

habitat: Red campion thrives in disturbed soils along roadsides, field edges, and woodland clearings throughout New England. It particularly enjoys rich, moist soil in partially shaded areas and is often found near old farmsteads, stone walls, and anywhere the ground has been disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge with their characteristic soft, hairy leaves arranged in opposite pairs. First flowers may appear in late spring as the plant reaches full height.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with clusters of bright pink flowers opening throughout the season. Plants are at their most visible and identifiable during these months.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature, splitting open to release seeds. Foliage may persist into early fall before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to ground level, leaving no above-ground parts visible until the following spring.

funFact: Red campion is 'dioecious,' meaning individual plants are either all-male or all-female - you'll never find both types of flowers on the same plant, making them like the plant kingdom's version of separate boys' and girls' schools!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with white campion, but red campion's pink flowers are the dead giveaway - white campion has pure white blooms. Both have the same inflated, balloon-like base behind their petals, but if it's pink, it's red campion!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'red' campion, the flowers are actually pink to rose-colored rather than true red. This is a common naming quirk in wildflowers, where 'red' often refers to any warm-colored bloom that isn't pure white or yellow.
compareHints: Red campion stands out from its Silene relatives by its bright pink color and preference for disturbed, rich soils. White campion is nearly identical except for flower color, while bladder campion has white flowers with a much more inflated, papery calyx that looks like a tiny balloon. Wild pink and fire pink are native species with more intensely colored, less notched petals.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its catchfly relatives, white campion stands out for being densely fuzzy all over, while most other Silene species are smoother.
Among the catchflies and campions in New England, bladder campion is the only one with those distinctive inflated, balloon-like sepals - this feature alone separates it from all its relatives.
Among its catchfly relatives, ragged-robin is unique for its deeply divided petals - other Silene species like white campion and bladder campion have whole, uncut petals.
Among its catchfly relatives, rose campion is unmistakable due to its completely silver-woolly appearance and intense magenta flowers.
Among its catchfly relatives, wild pink is distinguished by its extremely low, mat-forming growth habit and spring blooming time.
Among its catchfly relatives, sleepy catchfly stands out for having the smallest, least showy flowers that barely open.
Unlike its catchfly relatives that often have white or pale pink flowers, Maltese-cross blazes with intense scarlet-red blooms.
Unlike its taller relatives like white campion or bladder campion that grow as upright herbs in lower elevations, moss campion has evolved this unique cushion form specifically for alpine survival.
Among the catchflies and campions, starry campion stands out with its deeply fringed star-like petals and whorled leaf arrangement.
Among the red-flowered catchflies, royal catchfly stands out for its impressive height and late summer bloom time.
Among its catchfly relatives, night-flowering catchfly is unique for its extremely sticky, clammy texture and strict evening-flowering schedule.
Fire pink stands out dramatically from its catchfly relatives by its intense red color - most other Silene species have white, pink, or pale flowers.
Unlike white campion and bladder campion which have white flowers, sand catchfly's bright pink petals make it stand out.
Balkan catchfly is much smaller and more delicate than the common bladder campion, which has inflated balloon-like calyxes behind its flowers.
